stem: What is the difference between **sex** and **gender**?

options.content: Sex is biological; gender is social and learned
options.rationale: Correct: gender roles and expectations are learned.

options.content: Sex is learned; gender is biological
options.rationale: This reverses the two terms.

options.content: They mean exactly the same thing
options.rationale: They are different: one is biological, the other social.

options.content: Sex changes with fashion, while gender never changes at all
options.rationale: Gender expectations change over time; sex is biological.

explanation: Sex refers to biological differences; gender refers to the roles and expectations a society attaches to men and women.

options.content: Only women can give birth to children
options.rationale: This is a biological fact about sex, not a stereotype.

options.content: Girls are not good at mathematics
options.rationale: Correct: a fixed, over-simplified belief about girls.

options.content: Both boys and girls have a right to education
options.rationale: This is a right, not a stereotype.

options.content: Some pupils in the class are taller than others
options.rationale: This is not about gender at all.

explanation: A stereotype is a fixed belief about what a group can do. Many girls excel at mathematics.

stem: Which body is an independent commission that monitors gender equality in Zimbabwe?

options.content: the Zimbabwe Electoral Commission
options.rationale: ZEC runs elections.

options.content: the Zimbabwe Media Commission
options.rationale: This commission deals with the media.

options.content: the National Peace and Reconciliation Commission
options.rationale: This commission deals with peace and reconciliation.

options.content: the Zimbabwe Gender Commission
options.rationale: Correct: it monitors gender equality and investigates complaints.

explanation: The Zimbabwe Gender Commission is one of the independent commissions in Chapter 12 of the Constitution.

stem: In which year was CEDAW, the UN convention on ending discrimination against women, adopted?

options.rationale: Correct: CEDAW was adopted in 1979.
1989 is the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.
2003 is the Maputo Protocol.
2008 is the SADC Protocol on Gender and Development.

explanation: CEDAW 1979; Maputo Protocol 2003; SADC Protocol on Gender and Development 2008.

stem: A college offers a free bridging course in technical drawing to girls who never studied it at school, so they can meet the same entry standard for engineering. This is an example of …

options.content: gender discrimination
options.rationale: Discrimination treats people unfairly; this removes a barrier.

options.content: a gender stereotype
options.rationale: A stereotype is a fixed belief, not a support measure.

options.content: biological sex
options.rationale: Sex is biological and unrelated to a course.

options.content: gender equity
options.rationale: Correct: extra support to reach equal opportunity.

explanation: Equity means fair measures, sometimes extra support, so that both sexes can reach equal opportunities.
hints: Is the college giving extra support to reach a fair outcome?

stem: A company pays Rudo less than Farai for exactly the same job because she is a woman. This is …

options.content: gender equity
options.rationale: Equity is fair treatment; this is unfair.

options.content: gender discrimination
options.rationale: Correct: unfair treatment because of sex.

options.content: a gender role
options.rationale: A gender role is an expected task, not unequal pay.

options.content: a reserved seat in Parliament
options.rationale: Reserved seats are about representation in Parliament.

explanation: Paying a woman less for the same work because of her sex is gender discrimination, contrary to section 56.

stem: Why can **unpaid care work** be a barrier to gender equality?

options.content: It is illegal for women to do unpaid work
options.rationale: There is no such law.

options.content: It increases the wages that women earn in formal employment
options.rationale: It tends to reduce, not increase, time for paid work.

options.content: It leaves many women less time for paid work, study or leadership
options.rationale: Correct: time spent on care limits other opportunities.

options.content: It is done equally by men and women in every household
options.rationale: In many households women still do most of it.

explanation: Women often carry most of the cooking, caring and fetching water, which reduces the time available for paid work, study and leadership.
hints: Think about how many hours are left in the day.

stem: Which statement is the **most balanced** assessment of gender equality in Zimbabwe today?

options.content: Full gender equality has been achieved in every area of life
options.rationale: Overstated: barriers remain.

options.content: No progress has been made since independence
options.rationale: Wrong: there has been progress in education, law and representation.

options.content: The law is strong, but attitudes and daily practice lag behind
options.rationale: Correct: it weighs progress against barriers.

options.content: Gender equality is a matter that concerns women and girls only, not men
options.rationale: Wrong: it concerns men and boys too.

explanation: Zimbabwe has strong legal provisions and real progress, but stereotypes, violence, poverty and unpaid care work remain barriers.
hints: A balanced statement gives both progress and barriers.

stem: Gender equality is one of the founding values of the Constitution of Zimbabwe.
explanation: True. Section 3 lists gender equality among the founding values and principles.

stem: Gender equity and gender equality mean exactly the same thing.
explanation: False. Equality is the goal of equal rights and opportunities; equity is fair treatment, sometimes with extra support, to reach it.

stem: Match each provision or agreement with what it does.

right.content: UN convention to end discrimination against women
African protocol on the rights of women in Africa
promotes gender balance in government institutions
equality before the law and non-discrimination

explanation: Section 17 (gender balance), section 56 (equality and non-discrimination), CEDAW (1979) and the Maputo Protocol (2003).

payload.template: The SADC Protocol on Gender and Development was adopted in {{blank:a}}. The Maputo Protocol was adopted in {{blank:b}}.

explanation: SADC Protocol on Gender and Development 2008; Maputo Protocol 2003; CEDAW 1979.

payload.template: Reserving seats for women in the National Assembly is a measure of gender {{blank:a}} that aims at gender {{blank:b}} in representation.

explanation: Reserved seats are an equity measure (special support) aimed at equality (equal representation).
hints: Which is the means and which is the goal?

stem: Give the short name (abbreviation) of the 1979 UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women.
explanation: **CEDAW**: the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (1979).

stem: State **four** barriers to gender equality in Zimbabwe.

points.description: Any one of: cultural attitudes/stereotypes, gender-based violence, poverty, child marriage, unpaid care work, unequal access to land/credit/senior jobs, weak enforcement of laws, lack of awareness of rights
A second barrier
A third barrier
A fourth barrier

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Stereotypes, gender-based violence, poverty and unpaid care work.

stem: Explain **two** ways in which the Constitution promotes gender equality.

points.description: Identifies section 17 gender balance / reserved seats for women
Explains that it increases women's representation in government and decision-making
Identifies section 56 non-discrimination / section 80 / the Zimbabwe Gender Commission
Explains the effect, e.g. unfair treatment because of sex is unlawful; customs that infringe women's rights are void; complaints can be investigated

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Section 17 requires the state to promote gender balance, and seats in the National Assembly are reserved for women, which increases women's representation in decision-making. Section 56 forbids unfair discrimination on the grounds of sex or gender, so a woman paid less for the same work can challenge it, and the Zimbabwe Gender Commission can investigate complaints.

explanation: One mark for each provision and one for its explanation.
hints: Name the provision and say what it achieves.

stem: Suggest **two** ways a secondary school could promote gender equality, and explain each.

points.description: Suggests a practical measure, e.g. encouraging girls into science and technical subjects / boys into home economics
Explains that this breaks stereotypes and widens career choices
Suggests a second measure, e.g. sharing chores and leadership posts equally / gender clubs / careers days with role models of both sexes
Explains that pupils learn that both sexes can lead and do any task

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The school could encourage girls to take sciences and technical subjects and boys to take home economics, which breaks stereotypes and widens career choices. It could also share prefect posts and classroom duties equally and invite role models of both sexes to a careers day, so pupils learn that men and women can lead and do any job.

explanation: Credit sensible measures (1 each) with explanations (1 each).
hints: Think of subjects, duties and role models.

stem:
The table shows the leadership of clubs at a fictional secondary school in Gweru in two years (invented for this question).

| Year | Clubs led by a girl | Clubs led by a boy | Total clubs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | 3 | 9 | 12 |
| 2026 | 7 | 7 | 14 |

In 2023 the school began a mentoring scheme for girls and a rule that each club elects a chair and a vice-chair of different sexes.

Study the information and answer the questions.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Complete the sentence from the table.

payload.template: In 2022 girls led {{blank:a}} of the 12 clubs; by 2026 the number of clubs led by girls had risen to {{blank:b}}.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Identify **one** equity measure described and the gender equality goal it supports.

points.description: Equity measure: mentoring scheme for girls / rule on chair and vice-chair of different sexes
Goal: equal representation of girls and boys in leadership

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The mentoring scheme for girls, which supports equal representation of girls and boys in leadership.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain **two** possible reasons, other than the school's measures, why girls may still be less likely to stand for leadership in some schools.

points.description: Stereotypes that leaders should be male
so girls lack confidence or are discouraged by peers
Heavier household chores / unpaid care work at home
so girls have less time for clubs and meetings

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Stereotypes that leaders should be boys may make girls less confident or lead peers to discourage them. Girls often have more household chores at home, so they have less time to attend club meetings and take on leadership roles.

explanation: A data-based practice item (8 marks) on equity measures and leadership.
hints: Read the table row by row before you explain.

stem: This question is about gender and the law.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe **two** international agreements that commit Zimbabwe to gender equality.

points.description: CEDAW (1979): UN convention requiring states to end discrimination against women in law, politics, education, work and family life
Maputo Protocol (2003) or SADC Protocol on Gender and Development (2008), with its main purpose

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: CEDAW, adopted by the United Nations in 1979, requires states to end discrimination against women in law, politics, education, work, health and family life. The SADC Protocol on Gender and Development (2008) commits southern African states to gender equality in governance, education and the economy and to ending gender-based violence.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: "Laws alone cannot bring gender equality." How far do you agree?

points.description: For: attitudes, stereotypes and customs change slowly; laws are not always known or enforced
For: poverty and unpaid care work limit women regardless of the law
Against: laws have made real changes (Legal Age of Majority Act, reserved seats, Domestic Violence Act, equal property rights) and set standards
Supported judgement

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant points or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge and examples, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
There is strong support for the statement. Attitudes and stereotypes about what men and women should do change slowly, and many people do not know their rights or cannot afford to enforce them. Poverty and the burden of unpaid care work hold many women back whatever the law says.

However, laws have made a real difference. The Legal Age of Majority Act made women legal adults, the Constitution reserves seats for women and forbids discrimination, the Domestic Violence Act protects victims, and women can own property and land. Laws also set a standard that shapes attitudes over time.

I agree to a large extent. Laws are essential but not enough on their own; they must be combined with education, awareness, economic empowerment and changes in attitudes at home, at school and in communities.

explanation: A practice evaluative item on the role of law in gender equality.
hints: In (b), consider what laws have achieved and what they cannot change alone.
